inputs.script:
Under the hood, Stripe uses the token bucket algorithm.

Every user gets a bucket; each request takes a token,

and fresh tokens drip back in slowly.

If requests come faster than the drip, the bucket runs empty.

If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

The buckets live centrally, in Redis.

events.what: request 1 is admitted and takes one token
a fresh token drips back in
request 2 is admitted and takes one token
request 3 is admitted and takes one token
request 4 is admitted and takes the last token
request 5 finds the bucket empty and is rejected with 429
the next token drips back in

skills.why: The owning workflow; this plan is its Plan stage for one scene, stopped at Plan by the product
The props come from the source's own metaphor (bucket, token, drip), and each moment has a verb and a reason; rhythm is hold–hold–hold–burst–hold–pull-back
Each moment is cued to its narration line, with nothing shown before the line reaches it, and the scene ends on a held read; the windows are moments in one continuous scene, not cuts
One dominant motif (a token leaving with a request), with attention directed to one thing per moment
Choosing the scene shape (zoom-out-workspace-reveal) and the rules for the morph, lane, level, tag and camera

delivery.note: The worked example is mostly a full-frame diagram, so a voice-over with a hidden presenter, or a corner chip at the opening and close, would both work

content.question: How is a per-user limit actually enforced?
content.takeaway: Each request spends one token from its user's bucket; tokens drip back slowly, so a user who asks faster than the drip empties the bucket and the next request is rejected. Every bucket lives centrally, in Redis.

continuity.entry: The request rate limiter card at centre, full; no requests in flight

treatments.text: Few words on screen: the term 'token bucket — one per user', the labels 'one user', 'drip', 'API', the 429 tag and the Redis label. Narration never becomes on-screen sentences. Body type in Inter; the 429 status in the mono fallback.
treatments.camera: Held for m1–m5 so the token count can be read; one continuous decelerating pull-back in m6 reveals Redis and then locks. No other camera movement.
treatments.presenter: Undecided. The worked example needs the whole frame from m2 to m5; if the creator chooses a presenter, a small corner chip at m1 and m6 suits the diagram, and a hidden presenter suits it just as well.

The bucket size (3), the drip pace, the five requests and the other buckets' levels are illustrative; the source gives no values. Whether a small 'illustrative' note appears on screen is for the creator to decide
The brief leaves open whether this scene should follow the request rate limiter directly; the m1 reveal from the limiter's mark is designed to work in either position, so no resequence is proposed
The page colours rejection in a red that is not in the theme; this plan uses the accent for the rejected request instead

content.development: Open on the request rate limiter the viewer already knows and reveal that its body is a token bucket: 'under the hood' becomes a literal relabelling of the same object, not a new diagram. Then run one user's bucket as a worked example in close-up with the camera held still, so every change is on the objects: one request leaves with one token, one token drips back, a quick burst of three requests spends the bucket faster than the next drop can form, and a fifth request is refused with the 429 the viewer met earlier. A token drips back after the refusal, so the viewer sees the limit is a pace, not a ban. Only then does the single camera move of the scene happen: one decelerating pull-back reveals this bucket as one of many sitting inside a Redis store. Shape: the zoom-out-workspace-reveal blueprint, adapted — tight on the detail, micro-action in close-up, one pull-back to the containing whole, the frame locks.

demonstration.text: One user's bucket holds three tokens. Request 1 is admitted and spends a token; one token drips back. Requests 2–4 arrive faster than the drip and spend all three. Request 5 finds the bucket empty and is rejected with 429. A token then drips back in. The bucket is revealed as one of many per-user buckets in Redis.
